statement: As summarized by a 2004 narrative review of tablet analyses (Parrott, 2004), what is sold as ecstasy has mostly held MDMA but not always, and the amount in a tablet has varied widely. The review's estimates, which it calls very approximate, put the share of tablets holding MDMA at 90 to 98 in 100 from the 1980s to the early 1990s (the rest generally MDA), 50 to 80 in 100 in the mid to late 1990s (5 to 30 in 100 held MDA or MDEA and 4 to 20 in 100 other drugs), 80 to 95 in 100 in the late 1990s and values approaching 100 in 100 in the early 2000s. They rest on three large series (a US laboratory to 1985, where 87 of 89 samples submitted as ecstasy or MDMA held MDMA or MDA; Dutch monitoring from 1993; tablets in north-east Italy, 1995 to 2000) and on smaller surveys. In the Dutch series, 6 to 18 in 100 tablets in 1993 to 1997 held other drugs outside the amphetamine family, such as ketamine, atropine, caffeine or paracetamol; in Italy about 1 in 100 held nothing active. Other substances the review lists include opiates, dextromethorphan and 4-MTA, which the authors it cites say was implicated in four deaths in Britain and one in the Netherlands. The measured amount of MDMA also differed from tablet to tablet: 100 to 150 mg in most Italian samples; yearly UK averages of 90 to 102 mg (1991 to 1995) falling to 73 to 88 mg (1996 to 2001); and, within single small series, from under 20 mg to 140 mg (UK, mid-1990s) and from none (lactose) to 152 mg (Czech Republic). These are amounts measured in tablets, not amounts to take. For someone who felt little from a tablet, the analyses show that a tablet can hold much less MDMA than another, none, or a different drug. People in Australia who use ecstasy and were surveyed in 1998 to 2000 estimated that about 1 tablet in 4 or 5 was a dud, a ratio the review says is close to the more systematic survey data from Italy, the Netherlands and the Czech Republic. The review adds that jaw clenching, tooth grinding and the quality of mood changes are used to gauge a tablet's strength, and one qualitative study described early nausea as a sign; these are people's impressions, which the review does not compare with analyses. It says a tablet with MDA or MDEA in place of MDMA would probably not feel markedly different, except perhaps in how long it lasts. It does not look at other reasons for feeling little, such as tolerance, and has no data on what happens when people then take more; it says, without data, that tablets with a high amount may be especially risky for people new to MDMA. The limits are that no study used random sampling, most samples were brought in by people who use drugs or came from amnesty bins, seizures of uniform batches may overstate purity, a US service that charged $100 a pill probably over-represented unusual pills, and the data end around 2002, so they do not describe tablets now.
plain: Ecstasy is often MDMA, but not always, and one tablet can hold much more than another. A 2004 review of tablet tests put the share holding MDMA at about 90 to 98 in 100 from the 1980s to the early 1990s, about 50 to 80 in 100 in the mid-1990s, and nearly all by the early 2000s. The rest held related drugs such as MDA or MDEA, other substances such as ketamine, caffeine or paracetamol, or nothing active. The MDMA measured in tablets ran from none to about 150 mg (a measurement, not an amount to take). Some people feel a tablet did little. One possible reason, which these findings fit, is that it held less MDMA than the last one, or none. People in an Australian survey thought about 1 in 4 or 5 tablets was a dud. The review does not look at other reasons, such as tolerance, and has no data on what happens when people then take more. Its data end around 2002, the samples were not random, and it reaches us second-hand.
population: Tablets and capsules sold or submitted as ecstasy (or MDMA) and analysed in laboratories or by testing services in the USA (to 1985), the Netherlands (1993 to 1999), north-east Italy (1995 to 2000), the UK, the Czech Republic and a US website (to 2002), with surveys of people who use ecstasy on how they judged tablet quality, all as summarized in a 2004 narrative review
exposure: Being sold or submitted as ecstasy or MDMA; contents found by laboratory analysis (quick tests first in the Dutch series)
comparator: Earlier and later periods and different countries within the review; no random sample and no reference standard
outcome: Share of tablets holding MDMA, related drugs (MDA, MDEA), amphetamines or other substances; milligrams of MDMA per tablet
magnitude: Review estimates (very approximate), share of tablets holding MDMA: 90-98 in 100 (1980s to early 1990s; remaining 2-10 generally MDA); 50-80 (mid to late 1990s; 5-30 MDA or MDEA; 4-20 other drugs); 80-95 (late 1990s); approaching 100 (early 2000s). Dutch monitoring (several thousand tablets): MDMA alone 48-60 in 100 each year 1993-96, then 44 (1997), 75 (1998) and 81 (1999); each year 1993-96 MDEA alone 12-20, MDA alone 2-5, MDMA mixed 7-13, amphetamine alone 1-4, amphetamine mixtures 2-7; over 80 held an amphetamine-type drug; other drugs 6-17 (1993-96) and 18 (1997). Italy (at least 20,000 tablets, 1995-2000): MDMA 85-90, MDA or MDEA 8-10, inactive 1, others 1. Czech Republic (120 pills and capsules, 1998-2001): over 80 MDMA only. UK 2001 (136 tablets): all MDMA. US testing service 2002 (about 175 tablets): 88 MDMA alone or mixed, 4 MDA or MDE, 4 others, 4 no identifiable drug. US laboratory to 1985: 87 of 89 samples submitted as ecstasy or MDMA held MDMA or MDA. Amount per tablet as measured: Italy mostly 100-150 mg (1995-2000); UK yearly averages 90-102 mg (1991-95) and 73-88 mg (1996-2001); one UK series some 100-140 mg, some about 50 mg, some under 20 mg; Czech series 30-100 mg with 152 mg and 0 mg (lactose) at the extremes; one UK seizure of 80 tablets 73-89 mg (mean 79). People surveyed in Australia (1998-2000) judged about 1 tablet in 4 or 5 a dud (their estimate, not an analysis; the review says it is close to the more systematic survey data). Amounts are contents of tablets, not amounts to take.

evidence.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the 1970s to the early 1990s', 1st paragraph (p. 235); Table 1, Renfroe row (p. 236)
evidence.extracted: Renfroe (1986), as summarized: of 610 samples of MDA or MDMA among 20,721 street drug samples sent to a Californian laboratory between 1972 and 1985, 12% (89 samples) were submitted under the names MDMA, MDM, Adam, XTC or ecstasy. The large majority of those 89 held MDMA or MDMA with MDA; only two held neither (a capsule from Honolulu with an amphetamine compound, and a largely empty plastic syringe from Miami labelled ecstasy/speed). Table 1 gives 97% (n=87) containing MDMA or MDA.

evidence.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy during the mid-1990s', 1st paragraph (begins p. 235, ends p. 236); Table 2, Spruit (2001) 1993–1997 row (p. 236)
evidence.extracted: Dutch Drug Information Monitoring System, as summarized from Spruit (2001): set up in 1992; samples were not collected systematically, most being brought in by individual people who wanted to know what a pill held; each pill was quick-tested and those not identified were sent for laboratory analysis (on average more than 100 pills a week). In each year from 1993 to 1996 about 48–60% of pills held MDMA alone, 12–20% MDEA alone, 2–5% MDA alone, 7–13% MDMA mixed with amphetamine or other drugs, 1–4% amphetamine alone and 2–7% amphetamine mixtures without MDMA; over 80% held an amphetamine-type drug; 6–17% held other drugs outside that class (hallucinogens such as LSD and ketamine, atropine, caffeine, paracetamol or unknown compounds). In 1997 44% held MDMA alone, 14% MDMA plus another drug, 24% MDA, MDEA or amphetamine and 18% other non-amphetamine drugs; the review links the dip to difficulty in obtaining the chemical precursor. The share holding MDMA rose to 75% in 1998 and 81% in 1999. Table 2 gives, for 1993–1997, 44–60% MDMA only, 9–25% MDEA or MDA only, 16–25% mixtures and 6–18% others.

evidence.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 1st paragraph; Table 3, Schifano (2000), Spruit (2001) and Palenicek et al. (2002) rows (p. 237)
evidence.extracted: Italy, as quoted from Schifano (2000): forensic laboratories had examined at least 20,000 tablets in five years; about 85–90% of tablets seized in the north-east held MDMA as the active ingredient, in amounts of 100–150 mg a tablet; MDA and MDEA were usually in the remainder, phenylbutanamine occasionally, and dummy tablets about 1% of the material (Table 3: 85–90% MDMA, 8–10% MDA or MDEA, 1% inactive, 1% others). Netherlands 1999: around 81% held MDMA (Table 3: 81% MDMA only, 19% all others). Czech Republic, Palenicek et al. (2002): 120 pills and capsules analysed between 1998 and 2002 (Table 3 says 1998–2001), over 80% held only MDMA; the rest held amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDEA, ketamine, ephedrine, MDA or mixtures (Table 3: more than 80% MDMA, 4% MDA, under 16% others and mixtures).

evidence.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 2nd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'Hansen et al. (2001) noted'; it continues on p. 238); Table 3, Winstock et al. row (p. 237)
evidence.extracted: Hansen et al. (2001), as summarized: people in Australia who used ecstasy and were surveyed between 1998 and 2000 estimated that about one tablet in every four or five was a dud; the review says this ratio is close to the more systematic survey data from Italy, the Netherlands and the Czech Republic. Winstock et al. (2001) surveyed 1151 dance clubbers in June 1999 about beliefs, consumption and perceptions of quality; Table 3 gives subjective reports of recent improvements in the quality of supplies.

evidence.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 2nd paragraph, the part on p. 238 beginning 'The American website www.dancesafe.org' (the paragraph begins on p. 237); Table 3, Cole et al., Dancesafe and Ramsey (2003) rows (p. 237)
evidence.extracted: A US website, Dancesafe.org, listed tablets sent in for commercial analysis: about 175 tablets in 2002, of which 88% held MDMA alone or in combination and 4% held MDE or MDA (alone or in a combination without MDMA); Table 3 adds 4% others and 4% no identifiable drug. Ramsey et al. (2001): in samples from an amnesty bin at the entrance of a London dance venue, a high proportion of the tablets held MDMA and the powders were mostly amphetamine. Ramsey (2003), asked for later findings: the tablets in the bins were almost all MDMA. Cole et al. (2002): 136 tablets submitted to the Forensic Science Service in north-west England in 2001 all held MDMA by liquid chromatography.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'The non-equivalence of ecstasy and MDMA has been described')
evidence.extracted: The review's own estimates of the share of ecstasy tablets holding MDMA: from the 1980s to the early 1990s around 90–98%, the remaining 2–10% generally MDA; in the mid to late 1990s between 50 and 80%, with around 5–30% holding MDA or MDEA and around 4–20% other drugs; in the late 1990s around 80–95% (citing Spruit and Winstock et al.); in the early 2000s values approaching 100% in the most recent surveys (citing Cole et al. and Ramsey).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'These estimates can, however, only be seen as very approximate')
evidence.extracted: The review calls its estimates very approximate because the empirical evidence is limited: only three reports covered large samples over a long period (a US anonymous testing service, Renfroe 1986; the Dutch monitoring project, Spruit 2001; northern Italy, Schifano 2000), and the smaller surveys largely confirmed them. It adds that no study used a randomized sampling procedure; most samples were brought in by people who use drugs or came from amnesty bins; police seizures of large batches of uniform tablets may overestimate purity (Cole et al. 2002); and a US service charged $100 for each pill analysed (Baggott et al. 2000), far more than its street value, which probably led to a preponderance of atypical drugs.
evidence.quote: no study has employed a randomized sampling procedure

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'The non-equivalence of ecstasy and MDMA has practical consequences')
evidence.extracted: The review says that when a tablet holds MDA or MDEA, whose effects on brain chemistry are similar to those of MDMA, people would probably not notice any marked difference except possibly in how long the effect lasts or in subtle details of the experience (citing Hegadoren et al. 1999). In the Dutch data, even in the years with the lowest share of MDMA (1994 and 1997) the large majority of tablets still held MDMA, MDEA or MDA, and at other periods the match between ecstasy and MDMA was often around 90%.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'However, a substantial minority of ecstasy tablets')
evidence.extracted: The review states that a substantial minority of tablets held other compounds: between 1993 and 1997, 6–18% of Dutch samples held other drugs outside the amphetamine class. It says the effects of ketamine are so different from MDMA that taking it unknowingly could be extremely distressing, and reports that 4-methylthioamphetamine (4-MTA) was found in amnesty bins and, in the words of the authors it cites, had been implicated in four deaths in Britain and one in the Netherlands. A small proportion of tablets held weak substances (paracetamol, caffeine, placebo) and others held atropine, opiates, phenylbutanamine or dextromethorphan; the review says the acute effects of these could be unexpected and unpleasant.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'One intriguing question is why the supplies of ecstasy first became problematical')
evidence.extracted: The review says people who use ecstasy were fully aware of the quality problems of the mid-1990s and, when interviewed, can readily tell the occasions when they feel they have taken MDMA from their other experiences; jaw clenching, tooth grinding and the quality of mood changes are used to gauge the purity and strength of tablets, and one qualitative study described early nausea as a subjective sign. It adds that uncertainty over purity led many potential people to avoid illicit drugs, while regular ones often became more wary and took supplies only from friends. These are people's impressions; the review does not compare them with analyses of the tablets.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'Dosage is another important topic', pp. 239–240)
evidence.extracted: Amounts of MDMA per tablet, as summarized: most Italian samples held 100–150 mg in 1995–2000 (Schifano 2000); UK annual averages were 90–102 mg between 1991 and 1995 and 73–88 mg between 1996 and 2001 (Cole et al. 2002). Small UK studies in the mid-1990s found amounts that were variable and often low: some tablets held 100–140 mg, others about 50 mg and some under 20 mg (Sherlock et al. 1999). In the Czech Republic tablets varied from 30 to 100 mg, with 152 mg and 0 mg (lactose) at the extremes (Palenicek et al. 2002). 80 white tablets from a large UK police seizure in 2001 held 73–89 mg, mean 79 mg (Cole et al. 2002). The Dutch monitoring met high-amount tablets occasionally in 1998. The review calls unknown amount a key area of uncertainty, says that high-amount tablets may be particularly dangerous for people taking MDMA for the first time because they could cause a severe serotonin syndrome reaction (no data given), and notes that two sources found no analytic evidence of toxic contaminants in MDMA batches (King 2000; Schifano 2000).

risk_of_bias.note: No random sampling; samples were brought in by people, taken from amnesty bins or seized, and a paid test service over-represented odd tablets; the review itself calls its estimates very approximate.

inconsistency.note: The series agree on the pattern (mostly but not always MDMA; amounts vary); shares differ by place and year, which the claim reports as ranges.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: the primary analyses were not read, and the data end around 2002, so they do not answer what tablets hold now.

imprecision.note: Ranges without intervals; several series are small and the review's own estimates overlap.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive findings from observational analyses start low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each take a level, and the result is very low. The qualitative finding (tablets sold as ecstasy are often but not always MDMA, and the amount varies) is better supported than any single percentage. Status replicated: independent series in the US, the Netherlands, Italy, the UK and the Czech Republic point the same way, and the review reports their direction (METHODS 6.4). Stays at draft because it rests only on a narrative review (METHODS 6.3, 12). The claim is worded as a description of the years covered and gives no advice; the amounts are tablet contents, not doses.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on Parrott (2004) as summarized; none of the primary tablet analyses was read (Renfroe 1986; Spruit 2001; Schifano 2000; Cole et al. 2002; Palenicek et al. 2002; Ramsey et al. 2001), and none has a reference record here. SECTION: the brief put this claim in section 7, which only the senior author may write (the validator fails a section 7 claim whose drafter is not the senior author); it is staged in section 2, where METHODS 8 places drug-checking findings and adulterants. Move it if you prefer. VROLIJK 2022 (Vrolijk et al., Drugs, Habits and Social Policy, doi 10.1108/dhs-01-2022-0003) is still being obtained and was not used; it would add current years (2012 to 2021, against data here that end around 2002), a defined European sample (tablets sent to drug-checking services) and milligrams per tablet over time. RULE 0: the 'I barely felt it' paragraph is met for why it can happen (a weaker, empty or different tablet) but this review has no data on what happens when people take more; the editor may link the laboratory repeat-dose claim (cl_mdma_redose_cardiovascular) and the tolerance claim (cl_mdma_tolerance_chronic) from this one.
